lens: The absence of dedicated metabolomic age clock datasets forces a strategic pivot: leveraging the robust predictive accuracy (r > 0.92) and disease associations of proteomic clocks in biobanks like China (n=3,977) and Finland (n=1,990) as a scaffold to design metabolomic equivalents. This cross-omics framing could reveal whether metabolomic signatures capture unique aging dimensions missed by proteins or epigenetics, especially in multimorbidity.
known_to_ignore: Metabolomic age clocks can estimate chronological age
Biological age acceleration is linked to chronic disease risk
Epigenetic and proteomic clocks show high correlation with age (r > 0.8)
tensions: Proteomic age clock accuracy differs subtly between ethnic cohorts (Pearson r=0.92 in Chinese vs. 0.94 in Finnish biobanks), suggesting population-specific calibration needs
Epigenetic clocks like GrimAge show deceleration in severe COVID-19 (beta = -0.24), contrasting with typical age acceleration, indicating context-dependent clock behavior
gaps: Metabolomic aging signatures in East Asian vs. European populations, replicating proteomic biobank comparisons
Dose-response of environmental exposures (e.g., 0.03 mg/kg·bw·d) on metabolomic age, extending from epigenetic clock findings
Metabolomic clock validation in specific subgroups like parous women, where gravidity accelerates epigenetic aging (n=331)
reviewer_objections: No primary metabolomic age clock data is cited; all arguments rely on indirect proteomic/epigenetic evidence
Proposed cross-omics validation is speculative without pilot metabolomic assays in the referenced biobanks
Generalizability remains unproven due to lack of metabolomic-specific cohorts
next_extractions: Metabolomic profiling in the China (n=3,977) and Finland (n=1,990) biobanks to parallel proteomic clock studies
Quantify metabolomic age acceleration associations with the 18 chronic diseases identified in proteomic aging research
Test time-restricted eating (eTRF) interventions on metabolomic clocks, building on circadian gene effects seen in proteomic/epigenetic contexts
